blocks.h: 1. A. What the human element means in STCW

blocks.p: The human element is the complex of human factors bearing on the safe and efficient operation of a ship - competence, health and medical fitness, alertness and fatigue, communication, teamwork and leadership, safety culture, and the fit between the person and the task he is given. It is addressed by the International Convention on Standards of Training, Certification and Watchkeeping for Seafarers, 1978, as amended, whose Manila amendments entered into force on 1 January 2012 with full implementation required by 1 January 2017.

STCW does not address the human element by exhortation. It does so through mandatory standards in Part A of the STCW Code, working on two fronts: making certification depend on demonstrated ability rather than time served, and recognising that the seafarer is a physical human being with limits that no certificate overrides.

The central mechanism is the competence table. For each function and level, Part A of the Code specifies the competence, the knowledge, understanding and proficiency underpinning it, the methods for demonstrating competence, and the criteria for evaluating competence. A candidate is certificated because he has been assessed against a written standard, not because he has served a period.

ul: Regulation I/6 - training and assessment: those training and assessing must themselves be qualified for the task.
Regulation I/8 - quality standards systems: training, assessment and certification are continuously monitored, and Administrations are subject to independent evaluation.
Regulation I/11 - revalidation of certificates at intervals not exceeding five years, with refresher and updating training, so competence does not silently decay.
Chapter VI - safety familiarisation, basic training and instruction for all seafarers.

blocks.p: The Manila amendments made the most explicitly human-element additions by bringing the non-technical competences into the mandatory tables: leadership and teamworking skills, managerial skills at management level, and bridge and engine-room resource management - the recognition that a technically competent officer in a team that will not challenge him is still a hazard. Marine environment awareness and security-related training were added in the same revision.

The second front recognises the body. Regulation I/9 sets medical fitness standards and requires a valid medical certificate, with standards for eyesight and hearing and a bar on conditions likely to be aggravated by service at sea.
Regulation VIII/1 and Code section A-VIII/1 govern fitness for duty and are the provisions the question really points at:

ul: A minimum of 10 hours of rest in any 24-hour period, and 77 hours in any 7-day period.
Rest may be divided into no more than two periods, one of which shall be at least 6 hours, and the interval between consecutive rest periods shall not exceed 14 hours.
Musters, drills and inspections shall be conducted so as to minimise disturbance of rest periods and not induce fatigue.
Records of daily hours of rest shall be maintained and made available for inspection.
Exceptions may be permitted by the Administration within stated bounds, and must be recorded; they are not a general dispensation.
Prevention of drug and alcohol abuse, including a blood alcohol limit for seafarers performing designated safety, security and environmental duties.

blocks.p: Regulation VIII/2 and section A-VIII/2 then govern watchkeeping arrangements and principles, including the composition of the watch and, for the engine room, the conditions under which a periodically unattended machinery space may be operated.

blocks.h: 4. A. Responsibility placed on companies and Administrations

blocks.p: STCW deliberately places duties on the organisation, not only on the individual. Regulation I/14 requires the company to ensure that seafarers assigned to its ships hold appropriate certificates, that the ship is manned in compliance with the safe manning requirements of the Administration, that documentation is kept, and that seafarers receive ship-specific familiarisation and can communicate effectively and co-ordinate in an emergency.

The ISM Code reinforces the same ground from the safety-management side, requiring the company to ensure the ship is appropriately manned with qualified and medically fit seafarers, and to establish procedures for familiarisation and for identifying training needs. Administrations, for their part, approve training, issue and endorse certificates, and are themselves subject to independent evaluation - so the standard is audited rather than assumed.

blocks.h: 5. B. The IMO guidance on fatigue

blocks.p: The current IMO guidance at this examination is MSC.1/Circ.1598, Guidelines on fatigue, dated 24 January 2019. It replaced the earlier fatigue guidance and is a substantial rewrite rather than a reissue, reflecting the intervening research on sleep, circadian rhythm and performance.

Its structure is its most useful feature: it is organised into modules addressed to the different parties who can actually influence fatigue, rather than as a single text aimed at the seafarer alone. The modules cover, in substance:

ul: Fatigue itself - its nature, its causes, how it degrades attention, judgement, reaction time and decision-making, and why sleep loss accumulates as a debt that cannot be repaid by a single long sleep.
The seafarer - practical measures: sleep hygiene, use of off-watch time, the effect of caffeine, alcohol and diet, recognising fatigue in oneself and in others.
The master and the shipboard management team - designing watch schedules, planning port calls and maintenance so that work is not concentrated, and managing workload.
The company and the ship operator - manning levels, voyage and port scheduling, realistic administrative burden, and a culture in which reporting fatigue is safe.
The Administration - how to take fatigue into account in safe manning determinations, in surveys and in casualty investigation.
Training providers and those who design and build ships - accommodation, noise, vibration, lighting, motion and workspace layout all affect the quality of rest actually obtained.

blocks.p: It is important to classify it correctly: the Guidelines are recommendatory. They do not create obligations. They explain how to manage a risk that the mandatory instruments address only at the level of a minimum.

blocks.h: 6. B. How the guidance and the mandatory rules fit together

blocks.p: The mandatory rules set an enforceable floor - the rest hours in A-VIII/1, running in parallel with the hours of work and rest required by the Maritime Labour Convention, 2006, as amended, and with the manning and resource requirements of the ISM Code. The guidance addresses the risk that remains above that floor.

That distinction is the point of the whole limb, and it is worth stating explicitly: compliance with the minimum rest hours does not mean the crew is not fatigued. Rest hours can be met by a schedule that is nevertheless badly fragmented, timed against the body clock, or taken in accommodation too noisy for real sleep. Fatigue is also invisible to inspection in a way that a certificate or a rest-hour record is not - a tired officer looks like a rested one, and the record may show compliance that the watch schedule did not deliver. That is precisely why IMO addressed the guidance to every actor who can influence the outcome, from the naval architect to the individual on watch, and why in practice fatigue must be managed through the ship's safety management system - realistic watch schedules, port workload planning, honest rest records, and a reporting culture in which an officer can say he is too tired to take the watch.

Limb A is enormous - the human element in STCW could fill the paper - and limb B is narrow and specific. The failure mode is to write everything known about STCW and then two lines on fatigue. Four route steps for A and two for B keeps the balance, and the final step, which explains how guidance and mandatory rules relate, is the management-level judgement that separates a Class I answer from a Class II one.

blocks.h: The two-front idea that organises limb A

blocks.p: STCW attacks the human element on two fronts: demonstrated competence (what the person can do, assessed against a written standard) and physical limits (medical fitness, rest, manning). If you present limb A that way, every regulation you cite has an obvious home, and you will not produce an undifferentiated list of regulation numbers.

blocks.h: The sentence that earns limb B

blocks.p: Complying with the minimum rest hours does not mean the crew is not fatigued. Rest can be fragmented, badly timed against the body clock, or taken in accommodation too noisy to sleep in. That single sentence shows you understand why guidance exists alongside a mandatory minimum, and it is the natural bridge into the practical measures.

ul: Reciting regulation numbers with no organising idea. Group them: competence, fitness, duties.
Getting the rest hours wrong. It is 10 in 24 and 77 in 7 days, in no more than two periods, one of at least six hours, with intervals not over 14 hours.
Omitting the Manila additions - leadership, teamwork, managerial skills, resource management. They are the most explicitly human-element part of the Convention.
Treating the fatigue Guidelines as mandatory. They are recommendatory.
Confusing the STCW rest hours with the MLC hours of work and rest. They run in parallel and the MLC offers an alternative formulation based on maximum hours of work.
The Guidelines are guidance. Saying so, and then explaining why guidance is the right tool for a risk that cannot be inspected, is the mark of a good answer.
Exceptions to rest hours exist but are bounded and must be recorded. Candidates either forget them or treat them as a general dispensation.
The fatigue guidance is addressed to designers and Administrations as well as seafarers - a point almost nobody makes, and an easy distinguishing mark.
Do not date the STCW comprehensive review. At this sitting no revision had been adopted; asserting a session number or a target adoption year is a claim about a later period.
What are the minimum rest hours? - 10 in any 24 and 77 in any 7 days, in no more than two periods, one at least 6 hours, intervals not exceeding 14 hours.

How would you manage fatigue during a heavy port call? - plan the workload in advance, stagger the watch schedule, use shore assistance where available, defer non-critical maintenance, and record rest honestly rather than to the form.
Who is responsible for safe manning? - the Administration determines it and issues the safe manning document; the company must man the ship in compliance with it.

What is engine-room resource management? - the effective use of all available resources, human and technical, including communication, assertiveness, workload allocation and situational awareness; brought into the mandatory tables by the Manila amendments.
How does the ISM Code bear on this? - it requires appropriately manned ships with qualified, medically fit seafarers and procedures for familiarisation and training needs.

blocks.p: MEANING - COMPETENCE - FITNESS - DUTIES, then GUIDANCE - FIT. For the rest hours, the four numbers in order are 10, 77, 2, 6, 14 - ten in a day, seventy-seven in a week, at most two splits, one of at least six, never more than fourteen apart.

questions.understand_first: Most things that go wrong at sea go wrong because of a person, and for a long time the regulatory answer to that was simply to require more training. The deeper insight behind the modern rules is that a competent, well-trained officer will still make serious mistakes if he is exhausted, ill, working in a team that will not speak up to him, or operating equipment designed without much thought for the person using it. So the international response works on two fronts at once. The first is to stop treating training as time served and start treating it as demonstrated ability - a seafarer must show he can actually do the thing, assessed against a written standard, and that includes the social skills of leading a team and using all the resources on a bridge or in an engine room. The second is to accept that the human being has physical limits that no certificate can override: he must be medically fit, he must be rested, and there must be enough people aboard to allow that. Fatigue is where the second front is at its weakest, because it cannot be inspected the way a certificate can - a tired officer looks exactly like a rested one - which is why the rules on it are backed by guidance aimed at everybody who can influence it, from the designer of the ship down to the individual keeping the watch.

blocks.h: 1. What GISIS is, and the problem it solves

blocks.p: The Global Integrated Shipping Information System (GISIS) is a web-based information platform developed and maintained by the IMO Secretariat. Its existence answers a structural feature of the Organization: IMO has no inspectorate and no ships. Almost everything it knows about how its instruments are working in practice comes from what Member States report to it. Before GISIS that reporting was done by paper circular - slow to compile, scattered across documents, and very difficult to search or compare. GISIS consolidates into one system the information that States are required or invited to report under the various instruments.

It should be classified correctly at the outset: GISIS is an administrative platform, not an instrument. It creates no obligation of its own; the obligations live in the conventions, and GISIS is the channel through which they are discharged and the information made useful.

ul: To provide a single point of collection and dissemination for information related to IMO instruments.
To support Member States in implementing and enforcing those instruments, by giving Administrations and port State control access to information held by others.
To give the Organization the evidence base on which instruments are reviewed, amended and developed - so that policy rests on reported experience rather than assertion.
To promote transparency and information sharing between Administrations, and with industry where the data is public.
To reduce duplicated reporting, each item being collected once and made available to all who need it.

blocks.h: 3. The functions - how it works and what it holds

blocks.p: GISIS is organised into modules, each corresponding to a reporting obligation or a defined information set. Those in use include - and this list is not exhaustive - marine casualties and incidents; piracy and armed robbery against ships; reception facilities, including reports of their inadequacy; contact points for Administrations and national authorities; recognized organizations authorised by flag States; ship and company particulars; port State control information; and modules covering pollution prevention equipment, survey and certification, maritime security and facilitation.

The operating model is straightforward. Data is entered by designated national focal points in each Member State, and the Secretariat administers the system rather than generating the content. Access is tiered: some modules are open to the public, others are restricted to Member States or to registered users, according to the sensitivity of the data. Records are searchable and exportable, and that is the feature which converts a pile of individual reports into usable evidence. In doing so the system facilitates data sharing among Member States, letting one Administration see what another has reported without bilateral correspondence.

blocks.h: 4. The fuel oil module and MARPOL Annex VI

blocks.p: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 caps the sulphur content of fuel oil used on board - 0.50 % m/m globally since 1 January 2020, and 0.10 % m/m within emission control areas. But the Annex also recognises a practical reality: a ship cannot burn fuel that is not on sale. Regulation 18, on fuel oil availability and quality, therefore requires Parties to take reasonable steps to promote the availability of compliant fuel oil, and provides that where a ship cannot obtain compliant fuel oil despite best efforts, it reports that fact to its Administration and to the competent authority of the port of destination - the mechanism commonly known as the fuel oil non-availability report. Regulation 18 also provides for the ship to notify its Administration and the port State where a supplier has failed to meet the requirements, for example on the bunker delivery note or the representative sample.

The GISIS module collects these reports centrally. It should be distinguished from the separate Annex VI reporting stream under regulation 27, the collection and reporting of ship fuel oil consumption data, which is a different obligation with a different purpose.

ul: It gives a single standard channel and format, replacing ad hoc correspondence with several authorities in several forms.
The ship's own report becomes a preserved record, which is precisely what supports its position if the fuel used is later questioned at a port State inspection.
The report identifies the port and the supplier concerned, so it is actionable rather than merely noted.
Reports of genuine non-availability are kept distinct from reports of supply that failed to meet requirements - two different problems needing two different responses.
The Administration and the port State receive the same record, which removes an obvious source of dispute about what was reported and when.

blocks.p: The analytical value is much greater than the reporting value, because aggregation changes what the data means. A single non-availability report tells you about one ship on one day. Several hundred, searchable by port and by date, tell you something quite different:

ul: Where compliant fuel is genuinely unavailable - a map of the real supply position, as opposed to the assumed one.
Which ports recur, and which suppliers repeatedly fail on quality or documentation.
Risk-based targeting for port State control: inspectors can concentrate on ships that have bunkered where problems cluster, rather than inspecting at random.
Evidence for IMO in reviewing how regulation 18 is working and whether availability is adequate - the review of fuel availability is itself an obligation that needs data.

Separating genuine non-availability from evasion. This is the point that matters most to an honest operator: if a ship claims non-availability at a port where everyone else bunkered compliant fuel that week, the claim stands out - and conversely, a genuine claim is corroborated by the pattern.
Commercial use - bunker planning, supplier selection and voyage planning, where the data is publicly accessible.

blocks.p: A management-level answer must state the limitations, because they govern how much weight the data will bear:

ul: It is a reporting system. Its completeness depends entirely on States and ships actually reporting, and under-reporting is likely - a ship that quietly bunkers non-compliant fuel does not file a report.
Therefore the absence of reports from a port is not evidence that compliant fuel was available there. It may equally mean nobody reported.

Module membership and structure are administrative: modules are added, merged and reorganised without any instrument being amended, so any list of modules dates quickly, and the list above is given as non-exhaustive for that reason.

A GISIS record is evidence that a report was made, not a finding of fact. It does not determine whether the ship's efforts to obtain compliant fuel were genuinely reasonable - that remains for the Administration and the port State.

It supplements and does not replace the ship's own evidence: the bunker delivery note and its retained representative sample, the oil record book, and the correspondence showing the attempts made to obtain compliant fuel.

Splitting those into separate sections is the single easiest structural decision on this question, because most candidates blur them into one paragraph about 'usefulness' and only ever answer the reporting half. Closing on the limits of the data is what makes it a management-level answer rather than a description of a website.

blocks.h: The idea that makes GISIS explicable

blocks.p: IMO has no inspectors. It knows only what States tell it. GISIS exists so that what they tell it arrives in one place, in one format, and can be searched. Every aim and every function follows from that one fact, and so does every limitation - a system built entirely on voluntary reporting can never be complete.

blocks.h: Why aggregation is the real answer to 'usefulness'

blocks.p: One non-availability report is an anecdote. Several hundred, searchable by port and date, are evidence - about where compliant fuel actually is, which suppliers keep failing, and which non-availability claims look genuine against the pattern. If you make that point explicitly you have answered 'analysing' properly; if you do not, you have written the reporting half twice.

ul: Describing GISIS as if it imposed obligations. It is a platform; the obligations are in MARPOL Annex VI.
Answering 'usefulness' only in terms of reporting, and never addressing analysis.

This paper asks about the fuel oil module only. Do not drift into port reception facilities; a closely related question at another sitting asks for that, and this one does not.
A GISIS record proves a report, not a fact. Whether the ship's efforts were reasonable is still for the authorities to judge.

What would you retain aboard to support a non-availability report? - the correspondence with suppliers and agents showing the attempts made, the bunker delivery notes, the retained representative sample, the oil record book and the voyage plan.
Who enters the data into GISIS? - designated national focal points in each Member State; the IMO Secretariat administers the system.
What is the sulphur limit and since when? - 0.50 % m/m globally since 1 January 2020, and 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas.
How does a port State inspector use this? - to target inspections at ships that bunkered where problems cluster, and to test a non-availability claim against the pattern for that port.
Is GISIS public? - partly. Access is tiered, with some modules public and others restricted to Member States.

blocks.p: WHAT - AIM - FUNCTION for the first task; MODULE - REPORT - ANALYSE - LIMITS for the second. The examiner has given you two of the seven step names in the stem itself: reporting and analysing.

ul: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 - sulphur content of fuel oil; 0.50 % m/m globally from 1 January 2020, 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas.

questions.understand_first: A convention only works if the States that signed it can see what is actually happening. IMO has no inspectors and no ships of its own; almost everything it knows comes from what governments choose to send it. For decades that meant paper circulars - a State would report a casualty or a problem, the Secretariat would summarise it, and by the time anyone could use the information it was old and scattered. GISIS is the answer to that: one place where the information States are required or invited to report is collected, stored and made searchable, so that the same fact can serve a policy debate, a port State inspector and a shipowner planning a voyage. The fuel oil part of the question is a good illustration of why it matters. The rules cap how much sulphur may be burned, but they also recognise that a ship cannot burn fuel that is not for sale - so if compliant fuel genuinely cannot be obtained, the ship reports that fact rather than being punished for it. Those individual reports are not very interesting one at a time. steps.title: What GISIS is, and the problem it solves
points: Global Integrated Shipping Information System - a web-based platform maintained by the IMO Secretariat
IMO has no inspectorate; it depends on what Member States report
Before GISIS, reporting was by paper circular - slow, scattered and hard to search
GISIS consolidates the information States are required or invited to report
It is an administrative platform, not an instrument, and creates no obligation of itself

steps.title: The aim of the system
points: A single point of collection and dissemination for IMO-related information
To support Member States in implementing and enforcing IMO instruments
To give the Organization the evidence base for reviewing and developing instruments
To promote transparency and information sharing between Administrations
To reduce duplicated reporting by collecting each item once

steps.title: The functions - how it works and what it holds
points: Organised into modules, each corresponding to a reporting obligation or information set

Marine casualties and incidents; piracy and armed robbery; port reception facility inadequacies; contact points; recognized organizations; ship and company particulars; port State control; and others - the list is NOT exhaustive
Data entered by designated national focal points; the Secretariat administers
Tiered access - some modules public, others restricted to Member States
Searchable and exportable, which is what turns records into evidence
It thereby facilitates data sharing among Member States

steps.title: The fuel oil module and MARPOL Annex VI
points: Annex VI regulation 14 caps sulphur content - 0.50% m/m globally since 1 January 2020, 0.10% m/m in emission control areas
Regulation 18 - fuel oil availability and quality
A ship unable to obtain compliant fuel reports the fact, which is the FONAR mechanism
Regulation 18 also provides for notifying the Administration and port State where a supplier has failed to meet requirements
The GISIS module collects these reports centrally
Regulation 27 fuel oil consumption data reporting is the other, separate Annex VI stream

steps.title: Usefulness for reporting
points: One standard channel and format, replacing ad hoc correspondence
The ship's own report is preserved as a record supporting its position at a later inspection
The port or supplier concerned is identified, so the report is actionable
Reports of non-availability and of non-compliant supply are separated
The Administration and the port State both receive the same record

steps.title: Usefulness for analysing
points: Aggregation converts individual reports into a picture of where compliant fuel is genuinely unavailable
Identifies recurring problem ports and repeatedly failing suppliers
Supports port State control risk targeting rather than random inspection
Gives IMO the evidence base for reviewing fuel availability and the working of regulation 18
Distinguishes genuine market non-availability from evasion, which protects the honest operator
Useful commercially - bunker planning and supplier selection

steps.title: The limits of the data
points: It is a reporting system - its quality depends entirely on States and ships reporting
Under-reporting is likely, so absence of reports is not evidence of availability
Module membership and structure are administrative and change without any amendment
A GISIS record is evidence of a report having been made, not a finding of fact
It supplements, and does not replace, the ship's own records and the bunker delivery note

quick_revision.recall_15s: What. Global Integrated Shipping Information System - a web platform maintained by the IMO Secretariat. It exists because IMO has no inspectorate and knows only what Member States report; it replaced slow, scattered paper circulars. It is an administrative platform, not an instrument, and creates no obligation of itself. Aim. Single point of collection and dissemination; support States in implementing and enforcing IMO instruments; give IMO the evidence base for reviewing them; promote transparency and sharing; avoid duplicated reporting. Function. Organised in modules - casualties and incidents, piracy and armed robbery, reception facilities, contact points, recognized organizations, ship and company particulars, port State control and others; list NOT exhaustive. Data entered by national focal points; Secretariat administers; tiered access, some public, some Member-State only; searchable and exportable - which is what makes it evidence; facilitates data sharing between Administrations. Fuel oil module. Annex VI reg 14 caps sulphur - 0.50% m/m globally since 1 Jan 2020, 0.10% in ECAs. Reg 18 fuel oil availability and quality: a ship unable to obtain compliant fuel despite best efforts reports the fact to its Administration and the port of destination (the non-availability report), and may notify a supplier's failure to meet requirements. Distinguish reg 27, fuel oil consumption data - a separate stream. Reporting usefulness. One standard channel and format; a preserved record supporting the ship at a later inspection; identifies port and supplier so it is actionable; separates non-availability from bad supply; Administration and port State get the same record. Analysing usefulness. quick_revision.critical_regulation: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 - fuel oil availability and quality - is the regulation behind this question: Parties promote availability, and a ship unable to obtain compliant fuel oil despite best efforts reports that fact to its Administration and the port of destination, and may notify a supplier's failure to meet requirements. Regulation 14 sets the limits, 0.50 % m/m globally since 1 January 2020 and 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas. Regulation 27 fuel oil consumption data is a separate stream. GISIS itself is an administrative platform, not an instrument.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering 'usefulness' only in terms of reporting and never addressing analysing - the stem names both. The analytical answer is that aggregation turns individual reports into evidence about where compliant fuel really is and which suppliers keep failing. The second trap is inferring that no reports from a port means compliant fuel was available there; it may simply mean nobody reported. And do not drift into port reception facilities - this paper asks about the fuel oil module only.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the GISIS question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 what GISIS is and the problem it solves; 2 the aim; 3 the functions - modules, focal points, tiered access, searchability; 4 the fuel oil module and MARPOL Annex VI regulations 14 and 18; 5 usefulness for reporting; 6 usefulness for analysing; 7 the limits of the data.
retrieval_cards.why: The stem names 'reporting' and 'analysing' as separate verbs, so they must be separate sections. Most candidates answer only the first.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is GISIS and why does it exist?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Global Integrated Shipping Information System, a web-based platform maintained by the IMO Secretariat. It exists because IMO has no inspectorate and knows only what Member States report; GISIS consolidates that reporting into one searchable system in place of slow, scattered paper circulars. It is an administrative platform, not an instrument, and creates no obligation of its own.
retrieval_cards.why: The 'no inspectorate' point generates every aim, function and limitation.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which MARPOL Annex VI regulation underlies the fuel oil module, and what does it provide?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 18, fuel oil availability and quality. Parties take reasonable steps to promote availability; a ship unable to obtain compliant fuel oil despite best efforts reports that fact to its Administration and the competent authority of the port of destination; and a ship may notify its Administration and the port State where a supplier has failed to meet the requirements. Regulation 14 sets the limits and regulation 27 is a separate consumption-data stream.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming regulation 18 and distinguishing it from 27 is the precision the question wants.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is aggregation the real answer to 'usefulness for analysing'?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because one non-availability report is an anecdote, while several hundred searchable by port and date are evidence - showing where compliant fuel is genuinely unavailable, which ports and suppliers recur, where port State control should target, and whether a particular non-availability claim is consistent with the pattern or looks like evasion.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what separates the analysing half from the reporting half.

retrieval_cards.prompt: If GISIS shows no non-availability reports from a port, was compliant fuel available there?
retrieval_cards.answer: Not necessarily. GISIS is a reporting system and under-reporting is likely, so the absence of reports may simply mean nobody reported. A record proves that a report was made, not a fact about the market, and it does not determine whether a ship's efforts to obtain compliant fuel were reasonable.
retrieval_cards.why: The most attractive wrong inference available from this data set.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the Annex VI sulphur limits and their dates.
retrieval_cards.answer: 0.50 % m/m globally, in force since 1 January 2020, and 0.10 % m/m within emission control areas, which has applied for longer. Both are set by regulation 14 and both were operative at this sitting.
retrieval_cards.why: The numbers the fuel oil module exists to police.

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Two tasks in continuous prose. The first is descriptive - what GISIS is for and what it does. The second is evaluative and names its own two halves, reporting and analysing, which is the examiner signalling the structure. At management level the question is really testing whether the candidate understands what a voluntary reporting system can and cannot prove.
decomposition_gate.mark_allocation: No mark allocation is printed anywhere on this paper; recorded at 16 under printed instruction 2, and the question prints no lettered limbs. Weighting inferred from the two printed tasks: three route steps for aim and function, four for the fuel oil half, the extra weight reflecting that the stem names two distinct verbs and that the limitations are part of a management-level answer.
decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: GISIS correctly classified as an administrative platform rather than an instrument; a genuine statement of aim; the module and focal-point operating model; regulation 18 identified as the governing provision with the sulphur limits behind it; and separate, substantive treatment of reporting and of analysing, with aggregation identified as what gives the data value.

decomposition_gate.freshness_risk: MEDIUM - The regulations are long settled and the limits have applied since 1 January 2020. The risk is in the MODULE DESCRIPTION, which is administrative and dates quickly, and in the donor's MEPC references, which are all to sessions after this sitting.
decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. MARPOL Annex VI applies through the flag State and is enforced by port State control under an instrument of general application. No Indian statutory limb is asserted, so the Merchant Shipping Act boundary does not arise.
decomposition_gate.technical_ambiguities: The set of GISIS modules has no authoritative fixed list because membership changes administratively; the answer states the list as non-exhaustive rather than asserting completeness for a date it cannot verify. The stem's premise that GISIS 'recently' updated its fuel oil module is accepted as the examiner's own framing and anchored to the sitting, rather than being tested against a specific release date.
decomposition_gate.target_answer_shape: Seven numbered sections, three on aim and function and four on the fuel oil half, with the aims, the reporting benefits, the analytical benefits and the limitations each as bulleted lists, and the answer closing on what the data cannot prove.
